articles.full_text:
मानसून की एक्टिविटी कम होते ही प्रदेश में बढ़ी गर्मी और उमस, शनिवार से फिर छत्तीसगढ़ में एक्टिव होने की संभावना
तेज धूप की वजह से अधिकतम तापमान भी बढ़ा, शनिवार से लो प्रेशर सिस्टम बनने से मानसून की एक्टिविटी बढ़ने की संभावना
रायपुर: प्रदेश की राजधानी रायपुर सहित पूरे प्रदेश में पिछले चार-पांच दिनों से बारिश नहीं होने से उमस बढ़ गई है. मानसून की एक्टिविटी कम होते ही होते ही तेज धूप की वजह से अधिकतम तापमान भी बढ़ गया है. पूरे प्रदेश में अधिकतम तापमान की बात करें तो 30 से 35 डिग्री के आसपास जा पहुंचा है. मौसम विभाग के मुताबिक शनिवार को एक लो प्रेशर सिस्टम बनेगा जिसकी वजह से आगामी दो-तीन दिनों तक फिर से मानसून की एक्टिविटी में वृद्धि होने की संभावना है.
मौसम विभाग का क्या कहना है?
मौसम वैज्ञानिक गायत्रीवाणी कांचीभोटला ने बताया कि आज की स्थिति में मानसून द्रोणिका सतना से लेकर दीघा तक उत्तर छत्तीसगढ़ के ऊपर से जा रहा है. इसके साथ ही एक द्रोणीका सिक्किम से लेकर उत्तर ओडिशा तक फैला हुआ है. इस प्रभाव की वजह से कोई खास सिस्टम नहीं बना है. प्रदेश में अभी वीक मानसून कंडीशन बना हुआ है. अधिकांश स्थानों पर शुष्क और ड्राई मौसम रहने की संभावना है.
शनिवार से मानसून फिर एक्टिव होगा
मौसम वैज्ञानिक ने बताया कि एक्टिव मानसून कंडीशन शनिवार से लेकर आगामी दो-तीन दिनों तक रहने की संभावना है. इसकी वजह है यह है कि एक लो प्रेशर एरिया अंडमान में आगामी दो-तीन दिन में बनने की संभावना है. जो तीन-चार दिनों के बाद दक्षिण ओडिशा, आंध्र प्रदेश की ओर बढ़ने की संभावना है. इसके प्रभाव से प्रदेश में वर्षा की गतिविधि सक्रिय होने की संभावना है.
बढ़ा अधिकतम तापमान
अभी मानसून एक्टिव कंडीशन नहीं है. क्लियर स्काई कंडीशन देखने को मिल रहे हैं. जिसकी वजह से अधिकतम तापमान में वृद्धि हुई है. मध्य छत्तीसगढ़ में अधिकतम तापमान 33 डिग्री से 35 डिग्री के आसपास बना हुआ है. उत्तर छत्तीसगढ़ में 31 डिग्री से लेकर 33 डिग्री के आसपास अधिकतम तापमान बना हुआ है. दक्षिण छत्तीसगढ़ में अधिकतम तापमान 32 से लेकर 34 डिग्री के आसपास बना हुआ है.
अभी भी पूरे छत्तीसगढ़ से मानसून लौटने में लगभग 1 महीने का समय बचा हुआ है. आज की स्थिति में उत्तर पश्चिमी भारत राजस्थान के ऊपर से मानसून वापसी के फेवरेबल कंडीशन बन रहे हैं लेकिन छत्तीसगढ़ से मानसून वापसी होने में 1 महीने का समय बचा है.

Bengaluru: A day after
TOI highlighted how students spent up to 2.5 hours in school buses to travel a few kilometres on the Varthur-Gunjur stretch (SH-35), the situation on Friday was marginally better. Parents said schoolchildren remained stuck in long traffic queues on their commute home, maybe a few minutes less than Thursday. But stuck, they were.
Fresh complaints kept pouring in from citizens, particularly the large tech workforce residing along the corridor.
Amit Jain, a resident of the Varthur-Gunjur stretch, said his LKG-going child was stuck in traffic for more than an hour on Friday. “My child’s school is 4km from our home. While the school made some changes to student dispersal today, it still took over 1 hour and 15 minutes to cover the distance. Yesterday, the journey took nearly 2.5 hours,” he said.
Describing the ordeal faced by young children, Jain added: “The moment my child reached home today, the first thing he wanted to do was use the washroom. Imagine what these children go through while sitting inside buses for hours in traffic without any certainty about when they will reach home.”
Jain said the situation has left parents anxious and constantly monitoring school bus apps. “We keep worrying. Is the child OK? Is there a medical emergency? These are our thoughts. No parent should go through this stress every single day,” he said.
Parents’ frustration has spilled onto social media as well. One resident,
Arjun, posted on X that he eventually left home to pick up his daughter midway through her journey after tracking the bus’s slow movement.
“After waiting for nearly two hours, I picked up my daughter from the road. Otherwise, she would have taken another 45 minutes to reach home. I run an online business and had the flexibility to do that. What about parents who are in offices and cannot leave work?” he wrote.
Another resident, Neeraj Agarwal, said children should not be subjected to the hardships that many Bengaluru professionals have come to accept. Residents said unless bottlenecks along SH-35 are addressed and ongoing infrastructure work is expedited, schoolchildren will continue to bear the brunt of Bengaluru’s traffic woes.
boxKnee-jerk reactionBengaluru East City Corporation began filling potholes on portions of SH-35 using hot-mix asphalt. Civic officials told residents that pothole repair work would continue through Friday night, with the aim of improving driving conditions ahead of Saturday morning traffic. Residents dismissed the exercise as only a temporary fix. “Pothole filling is the bare minimum. Ongoing infrastructure work and larger issues causing traffic congestion remain unresolved,” said a resident.

articles.full_text:
My intention was to write about simple self-sufficiency, especially when it comes to growing food. But then this summer was challenging in a way in which I thought I was prepared for… but wasn’t. So I am interrupting my train of thought to reflect on one small awakening, but one which is becoming a loud wake-up call. The future we were all working so hard to avoid is here.
I have written about cultivating our food and running a farm business as a part-time slow waltz through joy and beauty. Not this summer. This summer, in 36° C heat, I obsessed and irrigated and fretted and sweated. Mostly I sweated. I didn’t have time to take time to stop to see the beauty. At night, I wilted into bed. I planted the zucchini in mounds of compost as I always do and the plants wilted even faster than I. The peppers took way too long to flower, though they did eventually. And don’t get me started about the salad greens in this heat. But the biggest setback was with my headliner, the black tomatoes. Though I seeded the summer vegetables in March, June and July did not produce a single ripe tomato.
I recently wrote about water as the limiting factor in cultivating our food. Without enough water, the intense heat has defeated the farms and gardens in my region. Though not publicized except in our farming journals, 60% of Italy is in drought conditions with the crops compromised or nonexistent. (Above: a river bed 10 km from my farm) But when my first tomato plant bit the dust in the heat—having been heavily watered—without a single fruit turning red, it changed everything. I spent the next few evenings sitting in the garden accompanied by a dog and a vodka, trying to sort out what I was missing.
I didn’t sort it out.
I needed to be taken by the hand and dragged back to the basics. It happened on our way to the village, when we often drive past a very large and very successful vegetable garden. I like to stop and check out what is growing and how. But last month I was shocked to see that the farmer had lost many of his summer vegetables to the heat. Most of his very large field had gone to grass. His tall staked tomato plants were still valiantly standing but were now covered within tarps. I laughed at the ridiculousness of this small and primitive gesture in the face of our brutal heat. But the next visit to town, I was shocked to see the farmer’s tomatoes were turning red. Under the tarp. Without sunlight.
Meanwhile, back at my farm, most of my tomato plants had lost leaves but still had brilliant green fruits. When they were pummelled by hail we were forced to cover them with an olive net. Enclosed in an environment with more humidity and less sunlight, the green tomatoes all began to turn red, giving us a deluge of delicious, juicy fruit. THIS was my epiphany.
What took me so long to figure this out? The tomato patch outside the village was covered by a net called a shade cloth. It comes in different levels of UV screening and accomplishes three things. It protects plants from the hail which bedevils us during rainstorms in very hot weather. It cuts back on the sunlight. And, when the ground is well-watered, the covering helps the tomatoes’ environment stay consistently moist. All the above stimulates the natural ethylene produced by the tomatoes which cause mature green tomatoes to fully ripen. Yes, sunlight is initially essential. And temperature. And fertile soil. And water. But water is not the most important factor as it turns out. Genetics is the bottom line.
The very simplified science: A growing green tomato is loaded with chlorophyll, the pigment we generally associate with the leaves, making the developing fruit appear green. Chlorophyll enables plants to capture sunlight, converting it to energy. When a tomato reaches maturity—and its seeds are viable—ethylene is released. The gas induces ripening through a genetically determined cascade of chemical changes. The chlorophyll breaks down, allowing the starches in the tomato to turn to sugars, and the orange, yellow and red pigments have their day in the sun. The increasing production of one of the pigments—lycopene, a carotinoid—begins to color the tomato red. All of this is by genetic design via changes over millennia The bright tomato color attracts predators to eat the ripe fruit. They then carry away the seeds to disperse elsewhere (with their feces as the perfect fertilizer). Attracting the animal is the plant’s way to disperse the tomato’s progeny.
All this I forgot with age and my hysteria over the tomatoes not ripening. The farmer whose tomatoes were ripening beautifully under a tarp, with no sunlight and increased humidity, probably learned from his grandparents that, in hot weather, the fully grown tomatoes would ripen if covered. This is also why, at the end of the tomato season, you can fill a bag with hard green tomatoes, add an apple (to stimulate the tomato’s ethylene release), close the bag, wait a week and find the tomatoes soft, red, and juicy.
The MIT Technology Review (August 13, 2026) projects the summer of 2027 to be even hotter as the U.S. burns through more fossil fuels and the current El Niño event continues. The effects will be even more significant next year. Whether or not I give up growing tomatoes in the increasing summer heat and move them to spring or fall, it is time I took some of my own advice and paid attention to the successful older farmers in my immediate area, in my community. They have heard stories (and some have lived through) catastrophic times; hail, snowstorms, droughts, famine, disease. They may not know the enzymes responsible for turning a green tomato red but they know tomatoes.
My gardens received a nineteenth century makeover. I removed most of the tomato plants from stakes, allowing them to vine horizontally—their natural habit. By placing them over low crates, the tomatoes were off the ground but low and horizontal. I did not cut off any suckers. They continued to grow and produce more large tomatoes. The bushier foliage protected the fruit from the sun and the ground was completely covered, holding onto the moisture. I cut off the growing tips of a few of the most fruit-laden plants and am rooting them (in beer bottles of water). I will pot them up when they have enough roots. If September remains very warm—as it is projected to be—I will plant them in a bed with only 5 to 6 hours of sun.
And I bought shade cloth.
I am not suggesting a specific action. I am sharing my story, what worked for me in the mountains, in the center of Umbria, in late August. Consider this a fable about changing times and the limits of what we can learn from books, the internet, and newspapers. It is about sailing into uncharted waters and the necessity of looking around our immediate neighborhood, our community, for answers specific to our region. It is also about pooling our knowledge instead of looking up generic answers on our phones.

articles.full_text:
Nurses report an ‘increase in deaths and maggots in wounds’ amid summer heatwave
Listen
5 min
Nurses report an ‘increase in deaths’ during the summer heatwave, finding maggots in wounds and cancer patients ‘dripping with sweat’, a survey has revealed.
The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) surveyed 2,471 nurses across the UK between August 12 and 28 on the impact of the heatwave this summer which saw temperatures reach highs of 38°C.
Nursing staff reported seeing an ‘increase in deaths’ across services, describing how patients ‘rapidly deteriorated in suffocating atmospheres’, with those suffering from heart failure and respiratory problems among the most vulnerable.
They described cancer patients ‘dripping with sweat’ during chemotherapy, while others reported finding maggots in wounds.
Nurses reported people in care homes ‘suffering’ in hot conditions, with ‘ineffective mitigations’ in place to keep older people and those with long-term conditions safe and comfortable.
Three in four respondents (74%) said they have ‘little or no confidence’ that the government is taking sufficient measures to reduce the impact of climate change on health and care services.
Now, the RCN is calling for work to start on installing cooling systems in all care homes, hospitals, and other settings before next summer. See box below for all their recommendations.
Related Article: Nurses asked to consult on guidance aimed at improving diagnosis of OCD and BDD
Testimonies from nurses highlighting the difficulty of caring for patients throughout the summer, with patients ‘suffering more from the effects of the heat’ than the original reason they had sought medical treatment.
A common theme reported by nurses was the impact of the heat on patients with failure and respiratory conditions.
One nurse in Wales said: ‘We had two frail patients for whom the extreme heat directly impacted their deaths.
‘Whilst it was not the only cause – if you are in respiratory failure, the heat is a death sentence.’
A nurse in the West Midlands also reported an ‘increase in deaths in the heatwave’, adding that they had to move ‘a patient out of the ward and into resus in the middle of the night to access the air-conditioning.’
Another nurse in the South East said: ‘I have actually cried for them [patients]. It’s inhumane.
‘I don’t think a veterinary surgery would be allowed to operate under such conditions.’
A palliative care nurse working in a South West hospital described finding maggots in a patients wound.
‘We had a palliative patient with chronic ulcers on the ward…the wounds festered enough that they attracted flies and were found to have maggots,’ she said.
‘Some of his and his relative’s last memories will be knowing of and, in his case, feeling maggots in his wounds.’
In one testimony, dubbed ‘shocking’ by the nursing union, a nurse reported increased respiratory distress in newborn babies with one children’s ward in Yorkshire reaching 44 degrees, according to one respondent.
The heatwave also impacted mental health patients, with one nurse reporting that patients were becoming ‘more agitated, aggressive and assaulting staff more.’
Related Article: RCN Foundation offers £1,200 grants for nurse wellbeing projects
Meanwhile, a nurse treating cancer patients in London said: ‘I’ve seen patients sweating and dripping due to the heat during chemotherapy.
‘There is no air conditioning running in the unit. During one particularly hot period, patients were visibly sweating throughout their treatment.
‘This feels like a safety concern, not just a comfort issue.’
The nursing union has now called for heat adaptations for health and care services to receive its own ringfenced funding from government, with the work ‘to start now’.
RCN’s general secretary and chief executive Professor Nicola Ranger, said: ‘This testimony reveals the devastating impact of extreme heat on patients, with increased death, deterioration, and conditions in services which, frankly, are an assault on people’s right to dignified, safe care.
‘The reality is that climate change is here, but long-term underinvestment in our health and care services has left them so unprepared.
‘Staff did everything they could in record-breaking temperatures to keep patients safe and comfortable, but they were fighting a losing battle in buildings which often lack even the most basic cooling facilities. It’s been incredibly traumatic.
‘We are all aware of the pressures that winter bring, but extreme heat is here to stay, and the clock is now ticking to accelerate investment in hospitals, care homes and other settings to ensure they are prepared.
Related Article: Greater investment needed in ‘fundamental’ nursing research, says RCN Scotland
‘This summer was our warning. By next, we need everywhere to have effective cooling facilities in place, or patients will suffer shocking harm once again.’
- Installation of cooling systems in all care homes, hospitals, and other settings before next summer
- Ring-fencing for heat adaptions for health and care services
- Relax uniform rules and manage use of personal protective equipment (PPE)
Source: The Royal College of Nursing

Highway builders seek extension of West Asia-related relief measures till December 31
NHBF has requested that the relief measures notified through the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways’ circulars dated April 1, April 17, April 25, May 18 and July 29 be extended up to December 31, 2026, or until prevailing abnormal market conditions substantially stabilise, whichever is earlier
NHBF said the measures have provided support to contractors and concessionaires and facilitated continued execution of national highway projects amid extraordinary and unforeseen market conditions.
The National Highways Builders Federation (NHBF) has urged the government to extend the relief measures provided to highway contractors and concessionaires for another three months beyond September 30, citing continued uncertainty in the wake of the geopolitical situation in West Asia.
NHBF has requested that the relief measures notified through the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways’ circulars dated April 1, April 17, April 25, May 18 and July 29 be extended up to December 31, 2026, or until prevailing abnormal market conditions substantially stabilise, whichever is earlier.
Advertisement
According to NHBF, the measures have provided support to contractors and concessionaires and facilitated continued execution of national highway projects amid extraordinary and unforeseen market conditions.
However, the federation said the circumstances that necessitated the relief measures continue to persist. It pointed to continued volatility in crude oil prices, fuel costs, transportation and logistics expenses and supply chains, resulting in financial and operational pressures for contractors and concessionaires.
NHBF warned that discontinuing the measures from September 30, while the underlying market conditions remain substantially unchanged, could create financial stress for ongoing projects, particularly those operating under constrained margins. It said this could also lead to avoidable claims, contractual disputes and project delays.
The federation has requested that any extension be issued on the same terms and conditions as the existing relief measures, without changes to their scope, eligibility or applicability.
Advertisement
NHBF said continuation of the measures would provide greater certainty to contractors and concessionaires, help maintain uninterrupted project execution during the period of market uncertainty, preserve the financial viability of ongoing contracts and facilitate timely completion of critical national highway projects.
Chetan Bhutani is a New Delhi-based economic policy journalist with ten years of experience in reporting and breaking stories about economic policy pertaining to India's infrastructure and financial sector, including highways, finance, railways, shipping, telecom, petroleum, and natural gas and currently works as an Associate Editor for Business Today TV. He is a journalist who works across multiple platforms and languages and offers in-depth coverage of the auto industry, regulations, new products, and reviews. Also, he has extensively reported about the actions taken by investigative authorities in relation to corporate and bank frauds as well as significant insolvency cases. Bhutani keeps a tight eye on all aspects of the government's public policies, from their creation to their implementation. In addition to his job, Chetan enjoys scheduling official appointments, travelling, going on road trips, playing cricket, and squash. Also, he is passionate about addressing climate change and road safety. He is a public policy enthusiast and has a master's degree in Public Administration.

Morocco’s weather service issued an orange-level alert Friday for thunderstorms, hail, high temperatures and strong winds affecting several provinces through Sunday.
Thunderstorms bringing 15 to 25 millimeters of rain, hail and strong wind gusts are forecast Friday in Tinghir, Errachidia, Midelt and Ouarzazate between noon and 11 p.m., the General Directorate of Meteorology said.
On Saturday, heavier rainfall of 30 to 40 millimeters is expected in Figuig, Jerada, Errachidia, Midelt, Boulemane and Tinghir between 11 a.m. and 11 p.m.
Temperatures are forecast to reach 38 to 40 C in Kenitra, Sidi Kacem, Sidi Slimane and Khemisset on Saturday and Sunday.
Tangier-Assilah and Fahs-Anjra are meanwhile expected to see wind gusts of 75 to 85 kilometers per hour over the weekend.
The weather service said unstable conditions could continue into next week, particularly across the Atlas, southeast and eastern Morocco.

Fans face heat at multiple events
Saturday will be mostly sunny, with temperatures in the mid-to-upper 90s. Many fans are expected to be out early Saturday morning for College GameDay, then head to the Grove to tailgate before going into the game.
Some natural shade from trees in the Grove is gone because of damage from January’s ice storm. Tents will be set up, but according to the report, they will not provide much relief.
Rowdy Staten, an Ole Miss student attending all three events Saturday, said he plans to prepare the night before.
“I guess drink a lot of water the night before to be honest, get all of those electrolytes in the night before. Just try to get into the shade, try not to be in the sun all day, kind of pace yourself being out as much,” Staten said.
Student section, visitor sideline face more sun
Fans sitting in the student section or on the visitors’ sideline will be in direct sun for most of the game. The sun will set just before 7 p.m., but that side of the stadium could be 10 to 20 degrees hotter for fans sitting there.
Vaught-Hemingway Stadium allows fans to bring in one sealed 20-ounce water bottle.
Fans are advised to hydrate before the game. Anyone drinking alcohol is advised to drink water between drinks, since alcohol increases dehydration.
